items.title: Epic wants Apple punished for following letter but not spirit of the ruling
items.content_html: By any measure, Apple is precisely complying with the ruling that the Epic vs. Apple judge put down about App Store steering and fees. In a filing to the US Supreme Court, Epic wants Apple punished for not following the spirit of the ruling, though. The next chapter of the saga begins on January 11, 2027 with oral arguments.

items.title: After more than 10 years worth of folding, the iPhone Duo still works
items.content_html:
As it turns out, you can damage your iPhone Duo by opening and closing it too much, at least theoretically. Don't worry, you don't have that much time on your hands.

Three weeks ago, CNET put the iPhone Duo on it's custom testing rig, the Fold-A-Phone. Now, after 440,300 folds, it's finally reached its breaking point.

Sort of, if you're willing to define "breaking point" loosely.

According to CNET, it still opens 90 to 95 percent of the way on the Fold-a-Phone rig. And if you open it by hand, you can still get it to open fully; it just doesn't feel as snappy as it used to.

CNET's readings and footage showed changes in how much force it took to open the phone around 390,000 folds. This included losing the distinctive snap it had upon opening it fully, and the hinge, perhaps unsurprisingly, was looser.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

The display still holds at other angles without issue. The lack of flatness does not meet CNET's criteria for failure, which would need to include loss of power, sensors failing to detect the screen where it needs to be within the given timeframe, or screen blackout.

As CNET points out, at 100 folds per day, 440,300 folds represents about 12 years of use, which is long past the practical lifespan of the iPhone Duo. CNET plans to continue testing the iPhone Duo.

items.title: 100,000 iPhone Duo apps is a start, but there's a long way to go
items.content_html:
Apple recently announced that over 100,000 apps have been built for the iPhone Duo, but with developers working with multiple SDKs, it could still be a long time before your favorite apps really make full use of what the first foldable iPhone has to offer.

At first blush, that 100,000 figure certainly grabs the attention, especially just a few weeks after launch. But it doesn't tell the whole story, and there's still work to be done.

While Apple's big number applies to apps that have been built from scratch or refactored to fully support the iPhone Duo, many more haven't. Yet more find themselves in some kind of middle ground.

Those apps don't look terrible on an iPhone Duo, but they don't look as great as they could. For that, some work will be needed.

That's the key here, because there is no guarantee that will happen anytime soon. Depending on who or which company makes the app in question, it might never happen at all.

In reality, apps in the App Store were split into three categories with the release of the iPhone Duo. To truly understand how that impacts iPhone buyers, we first have to get into what those categories actually are.

When you open an app on your iPhone Duo, there are three possible outcomes.

What to expect

When you open an app on your iPhone Duo, there are three possible outcomes.

Best-case scenario

If you're using one of those 100,000 apps Apple lauded in its press release, you'll get the best possible experience. The app will completely fill both the inner and outer displays, edge-to-edge.

The updated Google Maps uses the whole of the inner and outer displays on the iPhone Duo.

You'll also notice that the app features adaptive vertical navigation bars. The controls that would normally be on the bottom of the display now reside on the side, well within one-handed thumb reach. If you're right-handed, of course.

Apps like this are also built with Apple's Split View feature in mind, and are fully compliant. They'll work as expected when you use your iPhone Duo to multitask.

Most likely to happen

The second possibility is the middle ground. And while not quite as impressive as the best-case scenario, it's more than usable.

These apps resize to fill most of the iPhone Duo's inner display, but there are no vertical navigation controls to be found. The same also applies to the outer display, so the already squat display will be more cramped.

In fact, you'll get a big black vertical bar where the status bar lives on the right side of the display. The full width of the display won't be used as it would in the best-case scenario.

A terrible experience

The third possibility is one that users of older apps will likely be faced with. From my testing, it also affects apps from bigger companies.

Unfortunately, these companies are those less likely to rush to update their apps to make the most of the iPhone Duo. Especially considering its relatively small user base when compared to the rest of the iPhone lineup.

In use, an iPhone app like this appears full-screen on the outer display, just as it would on a traditional iPhone. But the navigation bar will remain in its usual position and not on the right side.

When the iPhone Duo is opened, you'll get something akin to using an old iPhone app on an iPad. That is, you'll see a small app in the middle of the display surrounded by large black borders.

Why this happens is all down to how, and when, the app was built.

The SDK trap

Apple gave app developers the tools they needed to make great iPhone Duo apps as soon as it was announced. The first Xcode 27.1 beta with iPhone Duo support was released on September 18, 2026, a little over a month before it went on sale.

Apps built using this too, against the iOS 27.1 SDK, are the ones that fare best. These are the apps built for iPhone Duo, and they make up the 100,000 Apple mentioned previously.

As has historically been the case, these tend to be apps from independent developers. But some big-name companies have gotten in on the act, some even before the iPhone Duo went on sale.

Apps built against the slightly older iOS 27 SDK make up that second section, the most likely home for your favorite app. These apps are certainly usable, but they don't offer the best experience that they could.

However, those apps are incredible improvements over apps built with pre-iOS 27 SDKs. Those are the ones that have no idea the iPhone Duo exists and look terrible as a result.

Apps that haven't been updated in months, and especially if it's been years, fall into this category. So do apps that have been updated but still use an old SDK, including some big ones.

Two that spring to mind immediately are the PlayStation and Xbox apps. Amazingly, the Nintendo app is a third.

Another notable app not to be updated to even fill the iPhone Duo display is Football Manager 27. That's despite the fact that it's a brand-new title at the center of a recent Apple Arcade press release.

A brand-new game that's being heavily publicized by Apple Arcade, yet no iPhone Duo support

I live in the UK, and the NHS app falls foul of this issue. A fact I'm reminded of every time I book an appointment with my doctor or order a prescription.

There are countless more, and the worrying thing is that these are apps that may stay this way for far too long. The people behind the NHS app probably aren't rushing to add iPhone Duo support, after all.

Support is not full support

There isn't much anyone can do about legacy apps, or those from developers not inclined to update them for the iPhone Duo. It's frustrating, but it isn't the only issue here.

The apps in that middle ground should also be a focus, and it's important that we don't allow developers to rest on their laurels. Apps filling the iPhone Duo's display shouldn't be the benchmark.

Instead, I think it's important that everyone remembers that apps can be better. Apps like Apple's 100,000 that make full use of the iPhone Duo's inner display, reworked navigation bar and all.

If developers are allowed to do the bare minimum and we settle for that middle ground, we risk another Apple Vision Pro situation.

Just as iPad apps work on Apple's headsets, apps built against the iOS 27 SDK also work on the iPhone Duo. But neither makes the most of what those two devices offer over anything else.

If the foldable iPhone is going to be the success the Apple Vision Pro isn't, it'll need great-looking apps along the way.

items.title: Designing HomeView was a hard but fun journey, says Apple
items.content_html:
Apple executives have revealed that the new HomeView is the culmination of years of design effort balancing audio, privacy, and especially Siri AI.

As the first buyers take delivery of the new HomeView, two of Apple's executives involved have been discussing the device. Speaking to TechRadar, they describe developing HomeView as a difficult but rewarding journey because of where it is meant to be used.

"Home life is super busy, you know, it's complicated, it's complex, and people are moving around," said Matthew Costello, Apple's Vice President of Hardware Engineering, "and we wanted a device that was really designed specifically for that environment."

Cecilia Dantas, Home Product Marketing, said that the overall goal was to "give you exactly what you need in the moment." She added that it was vital that HomeView "do that with absolute simplicity."

Dantas says the plan was always that each person's data be available to them, but privately. "It comes from your iPhone," she said. "If you leave, [if] you take your iPhone with you, it goes with you, and it's not kept on the device at all."

It's not intended to be just about calendars and reminders, though. Dantas says that she uses a shared family album on her HomeView, and it updates as others add to it.

HomeView can display photos on its screen when not in use.

"I'm really proud of the moments of connection that it brings," she said. "It is delightful to see the photos come up."

Long development

Costello said that ultimately HomeView "really was constructed around Siri." He said that Apple wanted to tie Siri AI into a "device that is communal in nature in a home."

"We thought [that] was a really important moment," he said. "Together with our Design Studio, we went on a long journey of exploration to figure out 'how do you create something that's a unique form for the home?'"

Despite Siri AI software being central to the design, the development actually started with the display. The company wanted a shape that "was unique from other form factors we have inside of Apple."

"So we ended up with the aspect ratio you see today," he continued. "That then drove a lot of decisions around where things were placed."

Learning from the HomePod

Chief amongst the components that had to be arranged within that form factor were the HomePod-like speakers. But it wasn't just a case of where they could fit, because the HomeView comes in two very different versions.

"Getting the display right with the audio, and then the split-audio architecture between having the sort of higher-frequency speakers in the head," said Costello about the main screen, "and then the lower-frequency woofer in the base was something we worked through."

"How do you then extend that to the wall-mounted version as well?" he asked. "It was a really fun, hard-fought journey to get to where we ended up."

HomeView's gets personialized information, such as calendar events, from your iPhone.

Beyond the speakers, though, Apple says that great attention was paid to the display. "I really love the fact that this is the lowest light performance we've ever engineered into a product," said Costello, "it's down to 0.3 nits."

"So officially, I represent the most dim product ever inside of Apple," he continued. "I don't know if that's a good or bad thing, but I'm super-happy about that."

Alongside the development of the hardware, Costello said that "we really custom-built this user interface for the home, so the apps and experiences that matter in the home setting are really front and center."

HomeView first reactions

AppleInsider's Andrew O'Hara agrees enough with Costello and Dantas that he says he wants to buy five HomeViews. But at the same time, he's found that it is obviously a first-generation device, and that it has clear faults alongside its equally clear potential.

items.title: Apple's canceled iOS multitasking UI lives on, with AI-enhanced emulation
items.content_html:
An unreleased iPhone multitasking interface, unseen for over a decade and a half, was brought back to life with the help of AI and emulation.

Before the iPhone got the app switcher we all know and love, Apple made multitasking available through a sliding drawer that popped up at the bottom of the screen. However, the company experimented with a much more impressive design, showing open apps as on-screen cards.

After AppleInsider described an Expose-like interface in early 2010, a special build of iOS 4 was discovered on an iPhone 4 prototype the very next year. In the decade that followed, nobody had ever showcased the card-like multitasking design - until an emulator developer used AI to bring the scrapped UI back to life.

In a Mastodon post, Steve Troughton-Smith shared a video of the unreleased multitasking UI, with a previously unknown build of iOS 4 running on a QEMU fork. The build number seen in the video is 8A218, which would make the operating system only slightly newer than the 8A216 build uncovered in 2011.

Post by @stroughtonsmith@mastodon.social
View on Mastodon

Artificial intelligence appears to have played a crucial role in getting the special build of iOS running. In a statement to AppleInsider, the developer said that "any old iOS build you can find is now something you can emulate, thanks to AI-assisted emulator development."

Based on available information, it looks as though this rare build of iOS came from a prototype unit rather than an internal restore bundle. In short, someone took the root filesystem of a development device or prototype iPhone, and then ChatGPT made it boot in QEMU.

The video itself offers a rare look at the Expose-style interface Apple was experimenting with during the iOS 4 development cycle. Each open application appeared as a card, taking up part of the screen. By double-tapping the Home button, users could easily switch between apps without scrolling.

Though the iPhone never got this card-style multitasking UI, Apple did end up bringing it to the iPad, in a manner of speaking. Before iPadOS 26 gave the platform windowed multitasking, the iPad app switcher similarly displayed open applications in the form of swipeable cards.

Still, the older iPadOS implementation is not identical to the planned iOS 4 multitasking UI, with app names appearing at the top rather than the bottom, for instance.

If it wasn't for artificial intelligence, we might never have seen the initial idea in action once again. The November 2026 video highlights the potential AI holds in the area of preserving unreleased or scrapped software designs.

Apple itself has recognized the significance of AI-assisted coding, with Xcode 27 introducing support for AI agents. Internally, Apple employees use AI for development as well, though the company has reportedly cut funds for third-party AI from $300 to $200 per engineer.
