items.title: Give your child more freedom with the right iPhone and iPad guardrails
items.content_html:
Apple's iOS 27 parental controls help you manage your child's apps, contacts, and screen time. Here's how to get started.

Technology, including iPhone and iPad, gives children opportunities to learn, create, and connect with others. Safety guidelines help them explore those possibilities while developing healthy habits.

Ideally, those guidelines should reflect each child's age, development, and readiness. Younger children need closer guidance, while older children can gradually take on more responsibility.

What children do on their devices matters just as much as how much time they spend using them. Thoughtful limits support creative activities while preserving time for sleep, homework, exercise, and family.

Apple's new parental controls, which came out with iOS 27, help families establish these boundaries. This includes contact management, app allowances, and device schedules.

You can think of them like guardrails that are there to keep your kids on the straight and narrow, while still giving them enough freedom for education, creativity, and knowledge. Combined with regular conversations, these tools give children a foundation for using technology confidently and responsibly.

Setting up these safety guardrails might be a bit intimidating, especially if you've never had to do it before. That's why we've come up with this helpful guide to iOS 27 Parental Controls.

Get ready

Let's talk about how you can make this entire process as painless as possible. Family tech administrative work is, frankly, no one's idea of a good time.

But we can make it easier by limiting pain points.

The very first thing you should do is pick somewhere relatively distraction-free for this whole process. I'd avoid living rooms or anywhere out in public; the last thing you want is to speed through menus because you can't focus, only to find out you missed something important.

The next is that your device, along with any child device you're setting up, should be updated to whatever the most current version of iOS or iPadOS is. This is especially crucial in the event that one device is on iOS 26, while the other is already on iOS 27.

By ensuring that both devices are on the same system, you can be assured that everything matches up correctly.

Charge both devices to full. You don't want to stop halfway through the process because you realized an iPhone is at 2%, and juggling cords isn't necessarily a stress-free activity, either.

I highly recommend that you plan on dedicating the back half of an afternoon to this process. It might not take you long at all, especially if you've already set up devices as part of your family group.

Or, it might take you a couple of hours to make sure everything is in the right place.

The nice thing, however, is that once you go through the process the first time, any subsequent setups are much, much easier.

Setting up a Family Sharing group and adding family members

Before you start anything at all, you'll need to have a Family Sharing group. You'll also need to be the person helming the group, or have access to that person's device.

On the administrator (parent) device, follow these steps:

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap your name
  3. Tap Family
  4. Tap Continue
  5. Follow the on-screen instructions to set up the Family Sharing group

While you're in that menu, it will give you the chance to add members during the setup process. However, there's a chance that you may already have created a Family Sharing group at one point, but may need to add new members.


Creating a Family Group on iOS 27

Here's how to add new members to your Family Sharing group:

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap the Add Member
  3. Tap Invite Others to add another member
  4. If your child already has a Child Account, enter their account password on your device to add them to the group
  5. If the child does not have a child account, tap Create Child Account and follow the on-screen instructions

From there, Apple will walk you through the process of setting up parental controls, location sharing, and more.

This may be where your journey ends. However, if you want to delve into granular safety settings, we've got you covered.

How to set safety settings for websites and apps on a child's device

The very first thing you should do, if you haven't done it yet, is start thinking about what apps and websites are child-appropriate. Fortunately, the App Store provides safety "nutrition labels" that say the recommended age rating and what in-app controls it offers.

If your child is 8 or older, we suggest discussing this with them directly. Tell them what kinds of apps you think are appropriate, and ask them what kinds of apps they plan on using.


Setting up Apps & Websites permissions on iOS 27

Ideally, the entire process should be done with your child involved, so they can understand what their limits and freedoms are.

And then, of course, after you have that discussion, the onus is on you to set up the guardrails.

Setting up Ask to Buy

Ask To Buy is an extremely handy feature. When enabled, you'll receive a notification whenever your child tries to buy or download an eligible purchase or download.

This doesn't just include apps. It also includes anything from the iTunes Store, Apple Music, or Apple Books.

If your child is under age 13, Ask to Buy will be enabled by default. However, it may be a good idea to enable it for older children; here's how to do that:

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap Family
  3. Tap your child's name
  4. Tap Ask to Buy
  5. Toggle on Ask to Buy

Additionally, you can set restrictions for both apps and Game Center features. This includes limiting apps by age rating, as well as controlling what your child can do with apps, including installing and deleting, making purchases, using App Clips, or playing in Game Center.

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap Family
  3. Tap your child's name
  4. Tap Apps & Websites
  5. Tap Restrictions
  6. Allow, block, or set restrictions for any settings shown

Enabling age-appropriate content restrictions

It's also a good time to make sure you've set age-appropriate restrictions on music, books, TV shows, and more. Again, Apple has already done the lion's share of the work for you.

Child accounts automatically have their content filtered by age. However, you can adjust them at any time by following these steps:

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap Family
  3. Tap your child's name
  4. Tap Content & Privacy Restrictions
  5. Allow or block settings shown under Content Restrictions

Restricting and allowing websites

All the app restrictions in the world won't make a difference if your child is having unfiltered access to the internet.

Apple automatically enables Approved Websites Only for children with a Child Account under 13. Limit Adult Websites is turned on by default for children with a Child Account under 18, or whatever the restrictions are for the country your child's account is registered to.


For younger children, it's recommended to allow only approved websites. Older children may only need adult content blocked

But there are going to be times when you may want to restrict specific websites or change settings. Here's how you can do that.

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap Family
  3. Tap your child's name
  4. Tap Apps & Websites
  5. Tap Restrictions

From there, you can set up the following:

  • Tap Approved Websites Only to only allow access to websites that you've approved
  • Tap Limit Adult Websites to limit access to detected adult websites
  • Tap Unrestricted to allow unrestricted access to websites

Managing who and how your child can talk to others

You can manage your child's contact list from your device, control whether they can add or edit contacts, and require permission before they communicate with someone new. Important: Your child must approve your request before you can manage their contacts.

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap Family
  3. Tap your child's name
  4. Tap Allowed Contacts

From there, you can view and make changes to your child's contacts. You can also turn on and off "Allow Contact Editing," which will send you requests to communicate with new contacts.


Choosing who your child can contact during Screen Time

You can also restrict when your child can call, FaceTime, or message others. You'll need to make sure Allowed Contacts is enabled, so be sure to follow the steps above.

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap Family
  3. Tap your child's name
  4. Tap Allowed Contacts

Now you can do the following:

  • Tap During Screen Time to choose who your child can communicate with during Screen Time hours
  • Tap When Device Paused or Unavailable to choose who your child can communicate with when their device is paused

Now, critically, you should turn on Communication Safety. This feature helps protect children from viewing or sharing photos with detected nudity, gore, or violence.


Enabling Communication Safety protects children from explicit content

Restricted content includes pictures and videos sent through a text message or a FaceTime Video Call.

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap Family
  3. Tap your child's name
  4. Tap Communication Safety
  5. Toggle on Communication Safety

Setting responsible screen time limits

Now that we've tackled what apps your child can use and who your child can talk to, let's discuss the next important part: when.

Screen time limits are critical for children, especially elementary-aged kids. But it's also important to realize that not all screen time is equal, either.

That's why we'll show you how to set up these limits, and how to exempt certain apps — and people — from being limited.

How to set up Time Allowances

Time Allowances let you manage how much time your child spends in different app categories, with Entertainment, Games, and Social Media included by default on their device. Time Allowances also features helpful tips, such as how much time to give each category.


Apple's Time Allowances suggestions were created in partnership with the American Academy of Pediatrics

You can adjust each category's time allowance, add categories, or move apps between categories to suit your child's needs.

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap Family
  3. Tap your child's name
  4. Tap Time Allowances

From there, you can do any of the following:

  • Toggle on Match Screen Time Schedule to use Time Allowances during certain times in your schedule
  • Drag the slider left or right to increase or decrease the amount of time your child can spend in an app category or on their device
  • Tap the name of your schedule to view or edit Time Allowances for different schedules
  • Under additional Time Allowances, tap or click the plus or minus buttons to create Time Allowances for apps that aren't assigned to a category

Screen Time Schedules let you set a custom schedule for your child's device use to fit your family's routine. You can choose which app categories, including Entertainment, Games, and Social Media, they can access at different times of day.

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap Family
  3. Tap your child's name
  4. Tap Screen Time Schedule
  5. Toggle on Schedule
  6. Tap Add Schedule
  7. Select the days where the schedule would apply

Once you've got a schedule set up, you can then:

  • Tap Add Time Window, then enter a new name, time, and allowed app categories to add a new time window to your child's schedule
  • Tap a time window, then modify the name, time, and allowed app categories to edit a time window in your child's schedule
  • Tap a time window, then tap Delete Time Window to delete a time window from your child's schedule

Now here's the critical part: setting up Always Allowed. Always Allowed is crucial for emergencies.

By default, essentials like FaceTime, Phone, and Messages are always available, so your child can reach you or anyone on their Always Allowed list. Here's how to manage Always Allowed.

  1. Open the Settings app
  2. Tap Family
  3. Tap your child's name
  4. Tap Always Allowed

From there, you can do the following actions:

  • Tap Add Apps, Add People, or Specific Contacts, then follow the on-screen instructions to allow an app or contact at all times
  • Tap the Edit or Remove button next to the app or contact to remove an app or contact

Growing together

Now that you've managed to get everything set up, here's where I get to break a bit of bad news to you: this process is never really finished. At least until you decide your child is responsible enough to handle unrestricted access to the internet or they turn 18, whichever comes first.

For younger children, you might find initial settings are too loose and need tightening down. For older children, you'll most assuredly find that some are overly restrictive.

It's a learning process for both you and your child. And no two children are alike, so don't automatically assume your first child's experience will be a particularly useful roadmap for any kids that follow.

The best thing you can do is maintain an open dialogue with your kids. As someone who grew up on the internet in a time when there were no guardrails, I can offer a bit of insight into what might help.

First, kids are going to accidentally — or intentionally — stumble into content you don't want them to see. Don't automatically assume that they're doing it to hurt you, themselves, or others.

Instead, if you notice this, approach them gently. Teaching a child to fear repercussions is a sure-fire way to get them to avoid telling you about any scary situation.

Tell your child what you expect of them. Explain why the rules exist, but don't frame it as your child not being smart enough or too untrustworthy to follow the rules.

Don't attempt to scare your child away from "bad" content. For certain kids, and for many teenagers, this just assures that the kids are going to go look for the content on their own behind your back.

Assume questions your child asks are in good faith. They may have a valid reason for relaxing screen time limits or wanting to use an app you may be on the fence about.

Fostering good communication with your child, especially when they're young, is a great way to set the precedent for your relationship going forward.

items.title: First HomeView and Apple TV 4K pre-orders are arriving
items.content_html:
Apple's latest home devices have begun being delivered to customers around the world, and will now be on sale in Apple Stores.

A month after Apple announced the updated Apple TV 4K and the new HomeView, the devices are finally arriving in buyers' hands. Both devices were unveiled on October 13, and preorders started immediately.

In our testing, the HomeView won't be for everyone, but it has huge potential. "It has big problems," wrote AppleInsider's Andrew O'Hara, "yet I want five of them."

By contrast, the new Apple TV 4K is outstanding and has just one problem. "Truly, top to bottom, there is a lot to love," wrote Andrew. "But honestly, it's incredibly hard to recommend everyone go out and buy a $300 streaming box. It's a lot of money, especially right now."

There are justifications for that price, continues Andrew. But perhaps this is one time when you really need to see the devices in action before buying.

In which case, it's good that both devices will now be on view and on sale in Apple Stores worldwide. If you do decide to buy, the physical retail stores are currently your quickest option, too.

That's because the Apple TV 4K and both versions of the HomeView are currently back-ordered online. The wall-mount version of HomeView now ships on November 17, 2026, for instance.

Both the HomeView with a base and the Apple TV 4K are currently listed as shipping in the range of December 1, 2026, to December 8.

Apple did announce one more home device alongside the HomeView and Apple TV 4K on October 13. That was the new HomePod mini 2, but that's been available since October 30.

So there have been buyers who have left theirs unboxed as they wait for the Apple TV 4K. Now is the time, then, to break them out and set up Apple's home theater surround sound system.

items.title: Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and more are inaccessible for millions
items.content_html:
Microsoft has suffered a global outage across most of its services which has now lasted more than 17 hours, and cut off services including Microsoft Exchange.

In October 2026, a change in Microsoft's Exchange Web Services affected Apple Mail. But now all of Exchange has gone down, as have multiple Microsoft 365 services.

According to the New York Times, the first problems were spotted at around 1:00 p.m. Eastern on Thursday, November 12, 2026. By 10:00 p.m., Microsoft reported that repairs were "not taking as expected."

Downdetector has been showing steadily falling numbers of reports of problems. However, it's likely that as people have learned of the news, they have stopped reporting their individual cases.

Microsoft is still reporting major problems across its services, and is posting roughly hourly updates on its status page. One update, now removed, reportedly said that Microsoft was seeing "early signs of stabilization."

The most recent update at around 6:00 a.m. Eastern was more positive. "We've made additional progress toward service recovery, with recovery actions completed across portions of the affected infrastructure in the Asia Pacific region," it says. "Traffic is being gradually restored, and we're seeing improvements in key customer scenarios, including mailbox access and delayed email processing."

"However, some users may continue to experience intermittent issues," it continues. "Our focus is now on extending these recovery actions across affected infrastructure in other regions, while continuing stabilization efforts and adding supporting capacity to improve service consistency."

This and at least most of the company's updates have repeated the same basic detail about the cause of the issue. "At this time, we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident," it says. "We will continue to treat this with urgency until full mitigation."

items.title: Apple HomeView review: Shallow launch, but incredible potential
items.content_html:
HomeView is Apple's first attempt at a smart home display, and while the potential is there, it has a ways to go before we recommend it for everyone.

There was no grand, on-stage introduction for HomeView. Instead, it was announced in a New York City loft, ripe with hands-on opportunities.

I was surprised there wasn't more fanfare. Cue the Jobsian theatrics. It's a smart home hub. It's a smart speaker. It's a photo frame.

They're all the same device: HomeView. I've been testing it out for more than a week and I'm not sure I've ever been more conflicted.

It has big problems, yet I want five of them.

Apple HomeView review: Classic Apple design

There are two versions of the Apple HomeView. There's a standard, countertop version and a wall-mounted version.

Apple HomeView review: Apple's new smart home dispay

Despite carrying the same price tag, the wall-mounted version lacks the base and larger external speaker. The countertop model comes in silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray while the wall-mounted model is exclusively silver and Space Gray.

I love the look of HomeView and think it blends into the home well. My other half also loves it, agreeing it's both "adorable" and "cute."

Getting new technology into the house isn't always an easy task, so having something that my partner finds both aesthetically pleasing and useful is a win.

The screen measures about six by six inches, or seven inches on the diagonal. Apple calls it an LED Liquid Retina display and it has a fingerprint-resistant coating, which does a decent job at keeping the display looking nice.

It has 500 nits of brightness, plenty for use indoors, but I think more importantly, it can go as low as 0.3 nits. Depending on your use case, this may be one of the most killer features of the HomeView.

Not even the Apple Watch can go that dim. By dropping so low, it is an ideal bedside companion. The screen gets so dark it won't disturb you while you're sleeping, but there is just enough visibility to see what's on the display.

No other smart display I've tested, like those from Amazon or Google, have gone this low. I hate sleeping next to a bright display, so this ultra-dim display is much appreciated.

Apple HomeView review: Taking a FaceTime call on HomeView

Within the somewhat chunky bezel is a 12MP Center Stage camera. It has very wide POV, easily keeping me in frame throughout the kitchen and zooms in to track your face.

Both models have four beam-forming microphones and speakers on the underside of the display. There's a speaker grille along the bottom edge of the display.

For the countertop version, the weighted base houses a second speaker system that absolutely provides richer, deeper sound. It's as good as a HomePod mini 2.

Apple HomeView review: Setting up HomeView with a nearby iPhone

There's a silicone pad on the bottom to prevent it from sliding around and the back has a USB-C port. In the box is a braided USB-C to USB-C cable to connect to the included 30W power adapter.

Internally, Apple is using its A18 processor. It's paired with 8GB of memory.

Apple HomeView review: Interface navigation

HomeView, as a new platform, has its own navigation flow to adjust to. It's a bit of an odd mashup of Apple Watch, Apple TV 4K, and iPhone, yet it's natural and easy to learn.

Apple HomeView review: Apple TV app

From your chosen face, you can swipe left and right to rotate between the different faces you've considered. If you swipe from the top-right, you'll open Control Center and pulling down from the middle invokes Siri AI.

Apple HomeView review: Side view of the countertop version

Dragging up from the bottom pulls into your app view. What is a little confusing is when or how you can customize all these different views.

The app view shows all the applications that you can use on HomeView but it also has widgets. Then you have your HomeView face, which also can potentially have widgets.

Apple HomeView review: App view with widgets

Apps can have light, dark, tinted, or clear appearances. You can change their order by dragging and dropping the app icons.

Oddly enough, Control Center isn't customizable. It is preset with brightness, volume, and other system controls but you can't change the layout or add extra controls.

Apple HomeView review: Faces and faces

Out of the box, HomeView has a dozen different faces to choose from. These will be the main view of your HomeView and where you come back to when not interacting with it.

Each of these faces have varying levels of customization and sometimes nifty tricks paired with them.

Home Camera: With this face, you can add up to nine live feeds of your Apple Home security cameras. The grid automatically adjusts based on how many cameras you have selected.

Home Modular: Another smart home-focused face, Home Modular lets you choose a combination of your Apple Home accessories, camera feeds, a clock face, and the intercom. It supports one of three layouts.

Photos: Photos shows random suggested photos, specified photos, or selected albums. This even works with shared albums.

Memories: Similar to the Photos face, this one chooses from your collection of photo memories to display.

Analog: A traditional, full-screen clock. You can choose with or without tick marks, with or without numbers, different sizes, and different colors.

Digital: Digital shows a digital clock and has configurations for colors, style, and font. It also has two spots for mini widgets.

Apple HomeView review: The flow face follows you as you move

Flow: With this face, it shows a colorful swirling background. Using the front-facing camera, it will track your movements around the room and react to them.

Snoopy: Like the other Snoopy faces Apple has released for Apple TV 4K and Apple Watch, the Snoopy face will show various animations, often reacting to the weather or holidays.

Modular: Unlike Home Modular, the standard Modular face can show four widgets in a grid, including home accessories.

Apple HomeView review: Fade face

Fade: Inspired by a sundial, the numbers fade in and out with the clock hand as it traverses the clock face.

Weather: See the current weather or the upcoming forecast, right on the HomeView

Calendar: See the current date and accent it with a color of your choosing.

One of my biggest problems with HomeView is that I love so many of the faces. Sometimes I want to use the security camera one while other times I just want it control-heavy.

I struggle between seeing Snoopy's fun animations, the forecast, or controlling my living room, bedroom, or kitchen lights.

It would be nice to have the face change throughout the day, possibly even tied to focus modes. For our main HomeView, I want to use the Modular face early in the day with our family calendar, the weather, time, and recommended home accessories.

Midday, it can change to something more elegant like the Fade face. To wrap the day, I want it back to a Modular face with the music widget, home accessories, and podcasts.

I think these faces should also adapt to your positioning in the room. We see adaptive faces a lot with thermostats that show limited content with a large font when you're far away so it's still legible, but then shift to more data-rich as you approach.

An easy way to pull this off is with screensavers. Snoopy could be a screensaver who fades away as you walk up to the display to control it.

Apple HomeView review: Multi-user support

HomeView supports up to six users. They are verified by facial recognition, and then their personal device if facial recognition fails.

When recognized, HomeView populates with your personal information across apps, like the calendar or Messages.

Enrolling works a bit like Face ID, where you tilt your head up, down, left, and right for it to get a complete scan. It's not as accurate as Face ID, but it works from across the room while Face ID doesn't.

Apple HomeView review: Setting up HomeView

Once enrolled on one HomeView, your facial scan is automatically used on all others so you don't have to scan your face each time.

To test, both my partner and I each enrolled our faces, then we'd take turns trying to get into one another's content. A few times we got close, catching glimpses of message content before it realized I had jumped in frame.

Sometimes it would still take a few moments for our personal content to load, which applies to widgets too. Widgets with personal information will be greyed out until your face is recognized.

Apple HomeView review: Apps and widgets

There are several first-party apps available on HomeView. Alarms, Calendar, FaceTime, Find My, Home, Intercom, Messages, Music, Podcasts, Reminders, Safari, Timers, Weather, and World Clock all come pre-installed.

Some Apple apps will show on HomeView alongside your other apps, but they are running from your phone. Right now, that includes Audiobooks, Apple TV, News, and Apple Classical Music.

It's kind of odd how these apps are broken out. I don't understand why Apple Music is native, but Apple Classical Music is not.

Apple HomeView review: Apple TV app

The same goes for Apple TV. You start pulling on that thread and things just get more confounding.

See, video and audio apps like Apple TV work on HomeView, but only if optimized to work with CarPlay. At the time of this review, there are no streaming services that support CarPlay and no confirmation any of them will.

I understand it from a practical standpoint. HomeView is intended to be used with quick interactions so you're not standing there playing a game on it.

By supporting CarPlay audio and video apps, it's one less new platform devs technically have to build for. Plus, the car shares similar usability guidance, i.e. quick interactions.

Not going to sugarcoat it though, I think it would have been more beneficial and simpler just to allow third-party apps, even if it limited the compatible categories.

Apple HomeView review: Some third party apps on HomeView

Currently, outside of Apple's apps, I also have Sofa, MLB, NYTimes, CarTV, and Spotify showing on HomeView. I expect this list to grow.

Besides full apps, there is one way for you to use third-party apps on HomeView — widgets. If an app supports the small widget format, it will (mostly) work on HomeView.

That's another shared commonality with CarPlay that also supports the small widget format. Any app's small widgets on your iPhone will automatically show on HomeView and you can add them to different faces.

This quickly unlocks a ton of functionality for HomeView and I'm not mad at all about this implementation. I've started adding a ton of different widgets to my HomeViews.

With the Oura widget I can see my sleep stages from the night before, Awaire shows my air quality, Carrot Weather is self-explanatory, and X shows me trending news stories. I also use a Dexcom G7 glucose sensor, so the Dexcom widget shows me my blood sugar all day.

Unfortunately, even though HomeView is repurposing existing widgets, not everything works. Dexcom for example, doesn't render the graph correctly if using a tinted face.

Some widgets are just shortcuts to the apps, so even if they show on HomeView they don't do anything. That's what I ran into with apps like Ring and SwitchBot.

Other apps seem to have problems with personal info. FedEx has a small widget but the content is blocked out. Kia's widget looks great with a lot of info, but the lock and unlock buttons don't work.

In the short term, I fear this is going to be a bit of a mess for users. It will be confusing as there are multiple levels of apps that work.

They could be native apps, CarPlay apps that run on HomeView, fully working widgets, widgets that load but can't be interacted with, widgets that accidentally hide personal info, and widgets that don't load at all.

Part of this is on lazy developers, but Apple can't escape its culpability for making this unnecessarily complicated. The good news is that this is all software-related and can be rectified with a bit of work.

There's no telling how long it will take for that to happen.

I'm a bit cautious with smart home displays trying to do too much. If they try to do everything, they end up being bad at everything.

I don't think it makes sense to truly open up HomeView to every third-party app out there. It will lose its sense of purpose and it still isn't an ideal device for gaming or checking your email.

Apple HomeView review: Playing a podcast on HomeView

There's a degree of inexplicable inconsistency with even Apple's apps though. Why is browsing Safari fine, but reading Apple News isn't?

Furthermore, I think it's shocking for Apple to develop a whole recipe manager and cooking interface for Apple News and not have it available on HomeView. Apple Watch is also meant for short interactions and glanceable info, but it has the Apple News app.

Maybe there's a compromise of eventually opening up HomeView to limited categories of apps. I think weather apps, smart home apps, news apps, AI chatbots, cooking apps, and video apps, among others would make sense to live on HomeView.

I should mention that the HomeView can be used with AirPlay. You can cast audio from the HomeView to other speakers or you can cast audio and video to the HomeView, which is at least something.

Apple HomeView review: Serious smart home chops

One of the standout features of HomeView is its smart home abilities. Like the Apple TV 4K and HomePod, HomeView will serve as a Home Hub.

A Home Hub for Apple Home users is what enables encrypted remote access, local video processing, and runs schedules and automations. It serves as a Thread border router too for your Thread mesh accessories.

I'm not sure if Apple did some secret magic to prioritize smart home control, but it is astonishingly fast. It's the fastest device in my home when it comes to controlling my Apple Home devices.

One accessory I have is the Channel Master Pro Floodlight in the backyard. It's aimed at our chicken coop and if we ever hear or see anything, we'll turn the floodlight on.

Apple HomeView review: Checking the front doorbell

We can see anything suspicious from the house and it provides functional light if we have to venture out there in the dead of night. It's a great light, but for my use, it needs a physical control.

When we see movement in the yard, by the time we open the Home app and get to the accessory, the intruder has almost always moved on. I've used a button in the past, but that still can have a slight delay to it.

HomeView, is next-level fast. It's one of the primary home controls I have on my Home Modular face.

One tap and before my finger has had a chance to pull away the light is already on. It's fantastic.

Cameras also shine, responding instantly and showing true live feeds on the Home Camera face. I can't express how much my partner and I love having a glanceable, always-on feed of the front door.

Sometimes I walk past only to realize a package had been delivered. And my partner appreciates being able to see who is at the front door before answering it without having to have their phone on them.

When I'm working in my studio, the Home Camera face lets me monitor the kids' playroom. There's so much utility.

I'm not sure if it's a bug or not, but the one problem I ran into is that passive home accessories cannot be added to the Home Modular face. Think contact sensors, environmental sensors, or presence sensors.

The reason I want them is that I have my own outdoor sensors. I have both a Netatmo Weather Station and an Eve Degree.

Rather than relying on publicly available weather data from miles away, I can use my own sensors. They show in the Home app on HomeView, but can't be added to the faces for some unknown reason.

The biggest problem that users will face with their smart home tech is lack of compatibility with other ecosystems. This is commonplace with smart displays. You can't use your Google Home or Apple Home devices with the Alexa Show or your Amazon devices on a Homey Portal.

What's most problematic here is that there is at least one big holdout. Amazon-owned Ring.

There are a lot of users out there who may use Apple Home but still use a Ring doorbell. Nest devices face a similar issue, at least the older ones before they started supporting Matter.

HomeView is designed for Apple Home users, and only Apple Home users. If you live in any other smart home ecosystem, HomeView won't add anything to your experience.

Apple HomeView review: Siri AI

Voice is a primary control for the HomeView. You can open apps, answer messages, play back music or a podcast, and get answers to questions.

HomeView has full support for Siri AI, complete with personal context. In all my testing, Siri AI was as fast as it ever was.

Some things, like smart home commands, did feel quicker than when I'm doing them on my iPhone.

It's very helpful to have the deep access to your calendar and messages. For example, last week I asked Siri when trivia was and it found the references in my texts.

Apple HomeView review: Siri AI on HomeView

I followed up the original message to track down where trivia was and then added it to my family calendar. Siri AI kept the original context of the conversation and properly responded to my follow-ups.

This works side-by-side with multi-user support. That way I can access my messages while my partner can access theirs.

Siri AI can answer general questions with deep world knowledge, which is better than on HomePod thanks to the display that can provide additional context when necessary.

It wouldn't be Siri without some odd missteps though. Several times I tried to set my good morning scene by saying "Siri, good morning!" and it just told me it couldn't do that from HomeView, even though I've done it before and set the same scene regularly from my HomePod mini.

Apple HomeView review: One-off features

Baked into HomeView are a bunch of one-off features that are cool on their own. They're great, but not big enough to pull out into their own dedicated sections here.

Take Intercom for example. This is the first time Apple has had a dedicated Intercom app on its devices. Intercom is native to the HomePod line and within the Home app.

From HomeView, you can speak to any person or room in your home. It's been increasingly helpful in my home since installing the HomeViews.

My partner can be up in the kitchen and use the intercom to reach me in the studio. Or if I'm not sure where my partner went, I can use the intercom to call for them throughout every HomePod or HomeView in the home.

Intercom also goes to the Home app, so your family members can be reached, even if they're outside. As long as they have their iPhone, Apple Watch, or iPad on them.

In all our testing, Intercom is quick, reliable, and has good audio quality. It's one of those features you start to use and get hooked on its convenience.

Another fantastic feature is cooking. Hold any recipe you find online near the HomeView and it will hand it off to your smart display.

Apple HomeView review: Cooking on HomeView

The recipe loads in Safari, but a cook icon appears in the lower-right corner. Tapping into this dedicated cooking mode, you can go through a checklist of ingredients and each individual step.

If there are timers within a recipe, they're highlighted and tapping on them will start the countdown. Multiple timers can exist at once with up to three showing as Live Activities at the top of the display.

Apple HomeView review: Cooking with pre-populated timers

I love how if you continue to use the HomeView, like moving to watch a TV show, the recipe exists as a Live Activity with the current step. So you can quickly tap into it to get back to your spot.

It didn't happen every time, but at least a few times I was able to inadvertently bypass paywalls with the cooking feature. It loads in Safari, but when I go into cooking mode, it pulled the recipe ingredients and steps without having an active subscription.

By being based around Safari, it does complicate some aspects of recipes. If you use a cooking app like Crouton, Paprika, or Saucepan, those apps aren't available on HomeView.

If you saved the recipe from online, you can just go back to Safari on your iPhone and it will still work. And any recipes you like, you can pin to come to later.

Mirror is a clever little trick when you're getting ready for the day. It lives in Control Center and when you open it, it activates the front-facing camera so that you can see yourself.

It's perfect if you're checking your hair or your fit before you head out the door. By default it is zoomed in on your face but you can also zoom out for a full-body view.

Apple HomeView review: Mirror app on HomeView

If you're an early riser and it's still dark, you can turn on the edge ring light. It's not super bright, but enough to add some extra lighting when necessary.

Apple HomeView review: Modular mounts

Officially, Apple offers up two wall mount options for HomeView. For both of these, it partnered with Schneider Electric.

Both wall mounts, one USB-C and one hardwired AC, are produced by Schneider Electric but sold by Apple and offered when buying a HomeView.

Apple HomeView review: Two versions of the HomeView wall mount

The mounts themselves are very similar to another. They have a hefty metal and plastic back plate that is covered by a white, silicone-covered face plate.

The USB-C version is just what you'd expect, a basic mount with a braided USB-C cable coming out of it. The cable is permanently attached and you can either drape it down the wall, or hide it within the wall before connecting to a USB-C power supply.

On the AC version, instead of a USB-C cable sticking out you have a power supply on the back of the plate with inputs for the ground, neutral, and hot wires.

I opted for the AC wired version because my plan was to remove one of my wall switches and put the HomeView in its place. I'd then swap out my regular bulbs for Philips Hue filament smart bulbs.

Apple HomeView review: Installing my HomeView into my wall

My HomeView would then act as the primary light switch for the ceiling lights. It would also control my GE Matter under-cabinet lights, and my living room smart lights.

Regardless of which mount you use, there is a male USB-C connector in the center that connects to HomeView. HomeView magnetically attaches to the mount, which requires substantial force to pull off.

The silicone pad and the USB-C connector in the middle add shear strength, so you will never accidentally knock HomeView off the wall as you pass. If you do need to remove it, it still comes off when necessary.

These two mounts are good if you plan on putting your HomeView on the wall, but I think HomeView has untapped potential. I wouldn't be surprised to see third party mounts and stands in the coming months from frequent Apple collaborators like Belkin, Satechi, or Twelve South.

In the meantime, I took it upon myself to create some. The first one I made was a swiveling stand for the countertop version.

Apple HomeView review: Custom spinning base for HomeView

Instead of dragging the silicone base across the counter, I made a three-inch stand with a bearing in the middle to let it effortlessly spin on my counter. It was a quick one-hour job on my 3D printer.

I had more fun with the wall-mounted version. I probably could have devised a whole new mount to replace the Schneider Electric one, but I took the easy way out.

Instead, I just created a curved back that went behind the existing USB-C mount. It then screws into place with two 6mm M3 bolts and has a common two-finger GoPro mount on the back.

Apple HomeView review: 3D printed GoPro mount for HomeVie

Using a GoPro tripod mount I had on hand and a spare mic arm, I turned the wall-mounted version of the HomeView into an elegant hovering smart display that looks great on my desk.

I can raise it up and down, left and right, and position it up against my monitor. It's amazing, and I love that I can use HomeView at my desk without having to take up any extra space.

You could also use this same mount in the kitchen by connecting it to an under-cabinet mount. That would make the HomeView an even better kitchen companion for FaceTime, recipes, or watching sports while cooking.

Apple HomeView review: I love having the display float above my computer

These 3D printed mounts and stands work well, but I am eager to see what others come up with. If any do release, they wouldn't require you to buy the expensive Schneider Electric wall mount either.

Apple HomeView review: What else we need

The more I've interacted with HomeView, the more I love it. Simultaneously, I also keep finding more little things that I want it to do.

I've already laid out several of them like scheduling faces throughout the day, sensors on faces, improved widget support, different mounts, and more.

Recent code leaks do point to some potential new features coming soon. Usually I wouldn't go into rumored features during a review, but I think they're important to how Apple could be developing this platform.

The first possible new feature is support for AI chatbots. This is an app category for CarPlay and would be trivial to add to HomeView.

Code references point to Apple actively working on this. I think that would be very useful to see ship.

The second new feature revealed in code is turning the HomeView into a HomeKit Secure Video camera. It would reportedly use the Center Stage Camera and act like other Apple Home security cameras.

There's a lot of nuance to it, but that would add a lot of value to HomeView. Plus, that means HomeView could be a motion sensor too.

You'd be able to configure automations to turn on the lights in a room whenever someone walks in and turn off when they leave.

To be super clear here, these features have not been announced and there is zero guarantee they ever will be. Their inclusion in the code suggests they could be coming, but don't be making purchasing decisions based on that.

Apple HomeView review: I'm cautiously optimistic

Here's the bottom line: HomeView is finally here. It's not perfect, but I genuinely love having it. It's what I've been waiting for for years now.

It's built for Apple users, and that's it. For better and worse.

At times, it's that Apple magic that makes it special. In my family, we share photos of the kids through a shared album in Apple Photos.

We tried using a dedicated photo frame to share them, but it required photos to be sent by email or through a manufacturer app that no one ever used. Now I can set up a HomeView for my parents with the shared album as the photo face and it will automatically update.

My house is fully powered by Apple Home devices. My shades, locks, HVAC, lights, fans, appliances, cameras, and more are all Apple Home compatible.

I've been jealous of the smart displays other ecosystems enjoy. I simply wanted a sleek, always-on display where I could see and control my home, preferably without getting bombarded with on-screen advertisements.

Apple has delivered that experience and much more with HomeView. It's just very, very shallow right now, and hard to recommend.

Now that it's here, I'm already looking to what's next. A larger version would be great.

While opinions very incredibly greatly on the screen size amongst the AppleInsider staff, the seven-inch display is perfect for me on the first model. I don't have room for anything larger on my desk or nightstand.

Rumors do say that Apple is working on a 9-inch version next. I think kitchens especially would benefit from that larger size.

But, we can't review hardware for the future. It has to be about now, and if you should buy it today.

As it stands, now, HomeView is buggy, limited in apps, and expensive for what it is and does. But I also want more of them.

Despite putting a wall-mounted HomeView only six feet from the kitchen, my partner has already requested another one to put on the kitchen counter.

I want one on my desk and another bedside so I'll have to do a gradual expansion of our HomeViews. Hopefully I can find them on sale.

Like I said, HomeView has great hardware, but the software has a ways to go. It's shallow, and Apple has a wealth of opportunity ahead.

Apple HomeView review: Pros

  • Sleek, compact, premium hardware
  • Fantastic support for Apple Home
  • Super customizable between faces, widgets, colors, & mounts
  • Siri AI works well
  • Lots of little touches

Apple HomeView review: Cons

  • No real third-party apps
  • No third-party video apps currently supported
  • No control for other smart home ecosystems
  • Software feels very early
  • On the expensive side

HomeView rating: 2.5 out of 5

How you rate HomeView is kind of how you perceive it. If you are an Apple Home user who wants a smart display that honestly doesn't do that much else yet, this is an easy 4 out of 5 rating.

If you aren't an Apple Home user, or want it for its other smart display capabilities, the rating drops down even lower than what I put on the piece here. It's capable, but certainly leaves me wanting more.

Both scenarios leave the rating room to grow, as Apple's newest platform gets its sea legs. The hardware is there, the software across the board just has to mature. A lot.

Where to buy the Apple HomeView

The Apple HomeView retails for $299, with retailers Amazon, B&H, and Expercom all carrying the smart home hub. Amazon, in particular, is offering a small discount on the device at the time of this review.

Check out our Apple HomeView Price Guide, which is updated throughout the day, to compare prices and view the latest availability.

items.title: Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Speed, Siri, and seriously expensive
items.content_html:
The new Apple TV 4K has landed, and it comes paired with new audio abilities, a fancy personalized AI assistant, and an eye-watering price tag that's hard to justify.

Apple's fourth-generation Apple TV 4K starts shipping four years after its predecessor. Quite a gap for Apple's hobby box.

As a streaming box, it already does quite a bit, and many new features can simply be delivered via software updates. Still, there was a growing list of requests from users, and I'm happy to see that Apple (mostly) listened to those requests.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Surprise, it's a small black box

Somehow, Apple managed to muster the courage and fight the urge to change the form factor of the latest Apple TV 4K. At first blush, it's identical in size, shape, and color to the last several models.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: The new Apple TV 4K fits right under or behind your TV

It's a squircle-shaped black puck with glossy sides and a matte top. There's a glossy Apple logo on the top surface.

When powered on, you'll see Apple repositioned the status light, from the lower-right corner to the center. There are also three far-field microphones; one on the front, one on the left, and one on the right.

Around back you have the limited selection of ports. There's your standard power input, HDMI output, as well as Ethernet.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: There are no longer two models of Apple TV 4K and it includes 128GB of storage, gigabit Ethernet, and Thread

Unlike with the prior generation, there is only one model of Apple TV 4K this time. That means Ethernet, Thread, and storage capacity no longer differentiate two distinct versions.

I think Apple's decision to limit Thread to the high-end model was a mistake last time and hurt adoption of the standard and led to market fragmentation. But we'll come back to that when talking about smart home.

Inside is Apple's A19 chip, a healthy upgrade from the old A15 Bionic. It also comes with 8GB of memory and 128GB of storage.

With a streaming box, I don't think a lot of people consider how much storage they do or don't need. Memory and SSD size aren't often advertised on Roku boxes, Fire sticks, or smart TVs.

Apple TV 4K does more than all of those though, and storage can absolutely get eaten up. My son loves playing games via Apple Arcade which start to add up, not to mention the requirements for Apple Intelligence.

128GB is enough that the vast majority of people won't have to worry about it. More die-hard users will find it enough to play with, given how tvOS is aggressive at clearing out user storage.

Apple says that the A19 chip offers up to 50% faster performance and the GPU is twice as powerful. The new chip finally has native AV1 decoding as well, a long-sought feature.

Several big streamers have been using AV1 encoding for content as it offers nearly 50% better compression than both H.264 and HEVC. That means you can get higher quality content using less data.

Netflix, YouTube, and Amazon Prime all stream some content in AV1. Just because Apple supports AV1 on the new Apple TV 4K doesn't mean you'll immediately see a benefit, as most apps will still need updates.

Finally on the hardware front, the latest Apple set-top box supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Like the last model, it supports Thread, which is now using version 1.4 as of tvOS 27.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Find my remote

Listening to Apple TV 4K users, the most requested feature I've heard has been improved tracking of the Siri Remote. It's great that Apple gave us not only Precision Finding, but audio feedback on the updated remote.

Apple doesn't explicitly state what it is using, but it's not using Ultra Wideband for the tracking. Precision Finding is limited to newer devices, which lines up with ones that have Bluetooth 6.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: It's easy to find the new Siri Remote

My assumption is Apple is using Channel Sounding, which works similarly to Ultra Wideband. It has centimeter-level precision when using the Find My app.

In my testing, it worked great on my iPhone 18 Pro. It was able to get a signal, even when my daughter hid the remote in another room.

Beyond Precision Finding, the remote can also chirp when lost. You can ask Siri on your phone, a nearby HomePod, or the Apple TV 4K itself to locate the remote and it will begin emitting a high-pitched beep.

There are no speaker holes on the remote as Apple is using a "tone inducer" rather than a traditional speaker. The chirp isn't super loud, but even when I buried it in a plush blanket or shoved it within the couch cushions, it was loud enough to hear from a few feet away.

Without any speaker holes, the new remote is externally identical to the older remote. It still has the same touch-sensitive click wheel at the top, back, TV, play/pause, mute, and volume buttons and it charges over USB-C.

I'm a fan of the Siri Remote and have no complaints over the updated version. The metal is cool and comfortable in the hand, it's got a good weight to it, and it's easy to use.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Surround sound audio

Another new feature for the Apple TV 4K (2026) is the ability to use four HomePod speakers at once. This is for a persistent setup and not one-off times casting via AirPlay as you could do before.

The last generation could only use a pair of HomePod speakers, though it did offer Dolby Atmos support. Using full-size HomePods, I found the bass to be a bit sloppy so I opted for a soundbar.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Four HomePods can be used as speakers for the Apple TV 4K

I did want to test the new four-speaker setup and I did so using four of the new HomePod mini 2 speakers. For this to work, you can use any combination of HomePod (2nd generation) and HomePod mini 2 as long as they are in matching pairs.

For example, you could use four HomePod mini 2 speakers or put two full-size HomePods in the front and two HomePod mini 2s in the back. Once the speakers are configured, the Apple TV 4K automatically prompted me to use the room's HomePods as the dedicated audio output.

Using the four mini HomePods, the audio was excellent. The Dolby Atmos spatial effect is noticeably better when you have actual rear speakers.

It also works better in a room like mine, where I have no back wall. Typically, the HomePods would try to mimic that Spatial Audio by bouncing the audio off the rear wall, but that was ineffective in an open-backed room as I have.

Apple also gives you the choice between true surround sound and Whole Room Audio. You can toggle between the two using Speaker Mode in Control Center.

Whole Room Audio plays the same audio from every speaker, which is great when you have a lot of people in the room and everyone can hear no matter where they are.

I also liked using Whole Room Audio at night. Even though Apple does have the Reduce Bass and voice enhancement adjustments, Whole Room Audio meant I could lower the volume and hear dialogue clearly from the speaker right behind my head.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Smart home & gaming

The Apple TV 4K is more than just a streaming box. It also acts as a smart home hub and, thanks to the App Store, a gaming system.

I'm a staunch Apple Home user and the Apple TV 4K has typically been my primary home hub since it's wired into my network. A home hub for Apple Home is what helps process your security camera footage, runs automations, and enables encrypted remote access to your devices.

With the new model, I didn't notice any speed improvements to my smart home devices, but everything continued to work as normal. It's a Thread Border Router too, beneficial for devices that use the self-healing mesh standard.

I think Apple TV 4K is less successful as a gaming system. Apple Arcade has an ever-expanding selection of games, but few larger titles.

Apple has convinced devs to bring a few AAA titles to its platforms in recent years like Cyberpunk and No Man's Sky, but none of them made it to the Apple TV 4K.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Setup screen for the new Apple TV 4K

This could have been the processor, as some of these titles need an A15 Pro at a minimum to operate. Maybe we'll see a shift now that we have the A19 processor onboard.

There have long been rumors of Apple working on its own gaming controller. The Apple TV 4K would be a great venue for that, alongside iPhone, iPad, and Mac.

In my dream world, I could purchase a game that would work across all my devices and I could move freely and continue my progress from Apple TV 4K, to my iPad, to my Mac.

Sadly, I won't be holding my breath for that experience any time in the near future.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Siri AI

Arguably, the best new feature for Apple TV 4K (2026) is Siri AI. It starts to bring the streaming box in line with HomePod mini 2, iPhone, iPad, and Mac.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: You can choose which version of Siri you use, as well as adjust its capabilities

Part of Siri AI works locally on the device while part of it is offloaded to a paired iPhone. You must have an iPhone with Apple Intelligence in the home to use Siri AI on the Apple TV 4K.

When set up, your Apple TV 4K will create a direct connection with your iPhone that is on the same Wi-Fi to process requests. It will also work if a device was recently on the same Wi-Fi but is now using cellular.

It does this because part of what Siri AI has access to is your personal information on your phone. Things like your messages, so you can ask "let's watch that show John just recommended."

It sounds a little funky and confusing, but in practice it's pretty simple. Setup was easy, I had to grant explicit access, and then it just worked.

Siri AI is not just personal knowledge, it also has much more broad world knowledge and information about some of the shows you watch. The former is straightforward, while the latter isn't.

I tried a bunch of questions and Siri AI gave me answers easily. It pops up in the corner of the display as it listens to me, tells me it's thinking, and then give me answers within a small popover or the full screen depending on what I'm asking.

I could ask about weather, sports, or just general questions about the world. I could also go back and forth with Siri AI.

One example I experienced was asking how the weather looked tomorrow. Siri AI gave me an answer, and I followed up saying "what about this weekend?"

Siri AI was able to retain that context and gave me the extra information.

Another example was while watching a show, I happened to see a short teaser for a new show, but I didn't see the whole thing or the name. So I asked "what's the new show Anthony Mackie has coming out?"

Siri AI asked if I was talking about 12 12 12, which I was. I followed up, asking if it had a trailer out yet, and it said yes before playing that trailer.

Finally, I asked Siri AI to add it to my watch list and wondered when it was coming out. All worked perfectly as expected and felt very natural.

Siri AI can provide information about what you're watching, beyond what it could do before. It is deep knowledge that was shocking at times.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Siri AI gave me detailed information about the Apple TV shows I watch

For example, I was watching Ted Lasso and I asked what sunglasses Coach Beard was wearing. Siri AI was able to give me the exact pair of Ray-Bans he was sporting.

You can also inquire about when a show was filmed, what's real and what's not, who different actors are, when new episodes come out, where scenes were filmed, what cars they're driving, and a whole lot more.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Siri AI is limited to seeing Apple TV content at launch

That comes with a big asterisk though. This currently only works with Apple TV content. Siri AI can't access other shows because of DRM limitations and it only sees a black screen.

Apple has opened this up to developers though, so there is a chance we could see more Siri AI capabilities come to other third party apps.

All of this I did, not using the Siri Remote, but using the new microphones on the Apple TV 4K. The three far-field microphones picked up my voice, even across the room.

This is another killer feature for the box because it was so easy to control media or get my questions answered. If my phone rings, I don't want to be looking around the room or even using Find My to locate the remote to pause my show.

The microphone on the Apple TV 4K is technically always-on, but when the Apple TV 4K is off, it is listening for keywords to turn on. Nothing else registers, saved, or recorded.

It's similar to how Siri works on your iPhone, iPad, or HomePod. That does lead to one interesting scenario, which is finding the remote while the TV is off.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Siri can help find the new remote that also has Precision Finding via Bluetooth 6 Channel Sounding

What you have to do is first wake up the Apple TV 4K, then ask it to find your Siri Remote. You can't find the remote via the Apple TV 4K microphones until it is turned on.

I do wish that Siri AI did a little bit more. Recommendations, for instance, felt a bit shallow.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Siri AI recommendations are good, not great

They were good, and apparently personalized, but seemed high-level. I asked for easy comedy shows to put on in the background and it suggested Ted Lasso, Ghost, Parks and Recreation, among others.

I believe this is the same recommendation engine we got with tvOS 27. I'd have loved to see an Apple Intelligence-powered on-device personalized recommendation engine that always had fresh shows and movies to recommend based on what I watch and what is trending.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Developers are the missing piece

As is often the case, a lot of the holes for Apple TV 4K are due to developer support. Devs have frequently shunned many of the Apple TV 4K native features that would make it even better.

Apple has provided easy solutions for logging into apps and assigning content to profiles, but few support all of these features. Netflix still doesn't support the Apple TV app queue or discovery.

I want to launch Hulu and have it automatically select my profile based on my Apple TV 4K profile, rather than make us choose each time. There's no reason developers can't do this, but almost every streaming app makes me choose who is watching.

As mentioned, we're also still waiting for bigger games to come to Apple TV 4K. Now, we have to wait for Siri AI support too.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: A lot of greatness held back by price

The new Apple TV 4K is outstanding. Truly, top to bottom there is a lot to love.

It is unequivocally the best streaming box you can connect to your television. It's fast, private, smart, powerful, and fun.

The speed is particularly noticeable with this update as the A19 chip flies. Opening apps, booting the Apple TV 4K, and starting videos all feel almost twice as fast as they were on my last-generation box.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: The new box looks just like the old one

But honestly, it's incredibly hard to recommend everyone go out and buy a $300 streaming box. It's a lot of money, especially right now.

There's some justification for that price. For example, memory prices have skyrocketed. TechInsights says NAND pricing has risen sevenfold since 2023 and the new box has double the memory and a whopping 128GB of storage.

If you look at component pricing, that would put Apple's COGS just for the SSD storage at roughly $30 in late 2026. If you accept a typical 4X modifier for determining MSRP, that one component contributes $120 to the price tag.

On top of that, there's Apple's custom silicon, premium construction, and the added costs of Apple's environmental efforts.

Looking to the competition, the Google TV Streamer is $149 but only has 4GB of memory and 32GB of storage. Not to mention it has only Wi-Fi 5.

Amazon has its most capable Fire TV Cube for $199 MSRP and it has 2GB of memory, 16GB of storage, only Wi-Fi 6e, 10/100 Ethernet (not Gigabit), and lacks Thread.

When you compare the Apple TV 4K (2026) to those, the price doesn't seem crazy. The problem is, those other devices frequently go on sale, and average consumers don't pay much attention to Wi-Fi specs, memory amounts, or the speeds of the Ethernet ports.

They don't need to. For most, video streamers to a television are appliances, not much different in the user's eye to the box that the cable company provides. In some cases, the Apple TV is the cable box.

Staring at a store shelf, Apple TV 4K looks very similar to the Fire TV Cube or Google TV Streamer for two to three times the price. At about $150, it was an uphill battle for Apple. It's just going to get worse.

Apple TV 4K is far better, more capable, and a better experience, especially for native Apple users. But what was only $69 a decade ago, now costs hundreds of dollars.

As a huge fan of TV and movies, I can justify it to myself. Not everyone can say the same.

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Pros

  • A19 chip is super fast
  • Excellent smart home hub for Apple Home
  • Four HomePod surround works and sounds great
  • Siri AI is a huge upgrade
  • Far more powerful than the competition

Apple TV 4K (2026) review: Cons

  • Price is going to be a dealbreaker for many
  • Siri AI will require dev support for video content
  • Still few apps that support Apple TV profiles, or AV1 decode
  • Gaming still largely overlooked

Apple TV 4K (2026) rating: 4 out of 5

Where to buy the Apple TV 4K (2026)

The 2026 Apple TV 4K sells for $299, with retailers Amazon, B&H, and Expercom all carrying the streaming box.

Set in 1970s New York, "Connector" revolves around a legendary ironworker who takes on forces greater than himself. The film is currently in development with no release date set.

items.title: Kid Cue is the iPhone Duo's secret weapon
items.content_html:
While some knock the iPhone Duo for perceived camera deficiencies, the Kid Cue feature might just be a big enough hit to make it worthwhile picking up for parents of kids young and old alike.

Like many, my choice of iPhone over the last decade or so has revolved around which cameras it has. As a parent of kids born in the mid-2010s, I wanted to be able to document everything in crystal-clear photos and videos.

The reality is that, despite what some might tell you, it's impossible to buy an iPhone that takes bad photos today. They're all great at it, and they have been for some time. The same goes for videos, too.

But there's no denying that models like the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max offer more flexibility. Even ignoring the new custom aperture situation, a real zoom lens is a big deal for some people.

The pro-tier paradox

With the iPhone Duo, Apple upset the natural order of things within its own lineup. No longer does paying the most money mean getting the best cameras.

If you want to pick up Apple's first foldable iPhone, you'll pay $800 more than an iPhone 18 Pro. Sure, it'll bend in the middle, but it'll take worse photos and videos in some circumstances.

This also means that if you do buy the model with the word "Pro" in its name, it'll be lacking. Pro cameras, maybe, but the iPhone Duo is the one that captures the imagination.

That's left a lot of potential buyers disappointed. But I'd wager that the iPhone Duo has a secret weapon, one that no other iPhone can boast.

Kid Cue uses the iPhone Duo's outer display to get the attention of kids when you want to take a photo or a video. And if you've ever tried to do either, you'll already know where I'm going with this.

The Kid Cue advantage

If you've ever been around kids, or dogs, for that matter, you'll know how difficult they can be. Things don't get any easier when you try to take a photo, no matter how many lenses or megapixels it has.

Kid Cue is Apple's answer to the age-old problem of getting a kid's attention long enough to snap a photo. When activated from the Camera app, Kid Cue puts a Snoopy-themed animation on the iPhone Duo's outer display to keep the child focused on the camera.

The iPhone Duo's Kid Cue mode is just a couple of taps away

While they're looking directly at the camera, you take the photo or capture your video. It's a simple feature, but one that should help avoid photos of kids looking in the other direction. The kind that litter any parent's Photos app.

Kid Cue is incredibly easy to use. And that's good, because you don't want to have to dive into settings when the chance for a great shot presents itself.

  1. Unfold your iPhone Duo with the inner display facing you.
  2. Open the Camera app.
  3. Tap the icon in the top-left that looks like the back of your iPhone Duo.
  4. Tap Kid Cue. The Snoopy-themed animation will play on the iPhone Duo's outer display to get your kid's attention.
  5. Take your photo or record your video as usual by pressing the shutter button or the Camera Control.

You won't get any of that with any other iPhone. And there's every chance it'll result in great photos that would otherwise never be taken.

Third-party alternatives

To be clear, Kid Cue is only available when using the official Apple Camera app preinstalled on the iPhone Duo. The feature isn't available for developers of other camera apps to use, but that doesn't mean that they can't get creative.

While apps can't hook into the Snoopy fun because there's no API available, they can mimic it. Developers are allowed to design their own attention-grabbing features using their own animations and graphics with the CameraCaptureAccessory and .sceneAccessory() APIs.

Whether they will or not remains to be seen. But the hope will be that Kid Cue is just the beginning, with developers using it as a jumping-off point for new ideas of their own.

A brave new world

The idea of the flagship iPhone no longer getting the best cameras is an alien one, that's for sure. But it's one that buyers will need to get used to, at least until bigger and better cameras can be squeezed into a foldable.

But the iPhone Duo's camera situation is more than serviceable, no matter what social media might tell you. And with that in mind, features like Kid Cue are very much welcome. The same goes for third-party iterations, too.

It could even be argued that despite its limitations, the iPhone Duo is the best iPhone for taking pictures of your family. It'll certainly help you capture shots of young kids that you might otherwise miss out on.

Just keep in mind that, for now, those shots might not be quite as sharp as they could be.

items.title: Donald Trump wants Tim Cook to be the next Nvidia CEO
items.content_html:
President Trump has weighed in on who he thinks Nvidia's next CEO should be, and he's picked another great big tech to do the job — Tim Cook.

The news broke early on Thursday morning about Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia. Whether he was told to quit or be fired, or if he made the decision himself may never be known.

Just the same, President Trump has chimed in on who he thinks should be Nvidia's next CEO. On a post on Truth, he has nominated Tim Cook for the job.

We got a screen cap of the post, just in case it changes or gets deleted.

Trump's post on Truth about wanting Cook to serve as Nvidia CEO.

It's not clear if Trump has talked to Cook about it, but that seems unlikely at this juncture. It's also unlikely that Trump has spoken to Nvidia's board about it yet, or if they will even consider the request.

Cook's got the chops to run the company, for sure. He probably also has significant non-compete clauses drafted following his exit from the role. Working for Nvidia would likely be a conflict.

And he's the chairman of the board at Apple. That seems to preclude the Nvidia job by itself.

If Trump does reach out to Cook, maybe Cook will suggest Johny Srouji for the spot. But maybe not, since he's done great work on Apple Silicon.

Not friends, but not enemies

During the first Trump administration, Cook was known for being close to the President, to a far greater degree than other business leaders.

During the term, Trump praised Cook for his communication skills, calling him a "great executive" due to repeatedly contacting Trump directly over important matters. While others used consultants, Trump was impressed by Cook's personal touch.

The term's famous US-China trade war was potentially damaging to Apple, but Cook led efforts to try and convince Trump from applying tariffs against its products. His influence certainly helped delay the application of tariffs, and did so altogether for iPhone, iPad, and Mac products when Trump signed a limited trade deal.

Outside of the trade war, Cook had visited the White House multiple times and discussed a wide range of topics with the world leader. Even a gaffe where Trump called him "Tim Apple" was taken in his stride.

And then, in Trump's second term as President, there's the "reciprocal" tariffs saga, that Cook spoke out against. That was followed shortly thereafter by the gold plaque gift.

Ultimately, those tariffs were ruled illegal. Apple has since received a series of refunds for those tariffs paid, which the company says will be reinvested in US manufacturing.
